part_title: Global Accelerator: Anycast Routing and CDN Comparison

scenes.title: AWS Global Accelerator
scenes.narration: Start with a global client connecting to the accelerator through a static anycast address. That same address is announced from multiple edge locations, helping clients reach a nearby entry point. From there, the AWS global network carries traffic toward configured regional application endpoints, shown as Application Load Balancers or Network Load Balancers in multiple Regions. The diagram distinguishes this network route from CloudFront content caching: Global Accelerator forwards traffic; it does not store an object at an edge cache. Endpoint health matters because the accelerator can stop routing new traffic to an unhealthy endpoint according to its configuration. The lower walkthrough creates an accelerator, adds a TCP or UDP listener, selects endpoint groups and supported endpoints, and examines the resulting static addresses. Those addresses are examples, not actual provisioned resources in the student's account. Use this service when regional failover, global network path optimization, or fixed IP entry points are useful for a supported application rather than when an HTTP object cache is the primary goal.

scenes.title: CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
scenes.narration: The comparison asks which problem you are solving. CloudFront is a content delivery network for HTTP and HTTPS applications, including websites, media, and eligible APIs. It serves cacheable content from distributed edge locations and forwards misses to S3, load balancers, or supported custom origins. Global Accelerator serves a broader class of supported TCP and UDP application traffic through static anycast addresses, using the AWS global network to reach healthy application endpoints. The two architecture sketches show CloudFront with an S3 origin and Global Accelerator with a regional load balancer. Look at the use-case row: static content and cacheable responses point toward CloudFront, while non-HTTP traffic or fixed address allowlists can point toward Global Accelerator. CloudFront can also serve dynamic HTTP traffic, so avoid claiming it works only for static files. The sample labs create one distribution and one accelerator to compare their different outputs: a distribution domain name versus global static IPs. Choose by protocol, caching requirements, endpoint types, and failover characteristics.
